content: Certain medications can interfere with the production of atidarsagene autotemcel. Patients should avoid taking antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) for at least one month prior to cell mobilization or for the duration required for the medications to be eliminated from the body. ARTs should also be avoided until all apheresis cycles are completed, as they may disrupt the manufacturing of apheresis-derived cells. Belzutifan can reduce the levels or effects of doravirine by altering its metabolism through the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored. If coadministration with belzutifan and sensitive CYP3A4 substrates cannot be avoided, consider increasing the dose of the sensitive substrate as per its prescribing information. Bexarotene, bosentan, brigatinib, butabarbital, butalbital, carbamazepine, dabrafenib, efavirenz, encorafenib, enzalutamide, eslicarbazepine acetate, etravirine, lumacaftor/ivacaftor, mitotane, nafcillin, nevirapine, oxcarbazepine, pentobarbital, phenobarbital, phenytoin, primidone, rifampin, rifapentine, and St. John’s Wort are contraindicated with doravirine. These drugs decrease doravirine levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially leading to a loss of virologic response and resistance to doravirine. Caution is advised when coadministering doravirine with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ceritinib, chloramphenicol, clarithromycin, cobicistat, conivaptan, darunavir, fedratinib, fexinidazole, fosamprenavir, grapefruit, idelalisib, imatinib, indinavir, isoniazid, itraconazole, lenacapavir, lopinavir, nefazodone, nelfinavir, posaconazole, ritonavir, stiripentol, tipranavir, and voriconazole. These inhibitors may increase doravirine plasma concentrations and toxicities. Dosage adjustments or close monitoring may be required. Elagolix, cenobamate, and tazemetostat may decrease doravirine levels or effects by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored, and dose adjustments of CYP3A4 substrates may be necessary. Patients undergoing treatment with doravirine should be aware of the potential for immune reconstitution syndrome, which may result in an inflammatory response to latent or residual opportunistic infections such as Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis. Autoimmune disorders, including Graves’ disease, polymyositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and autoimmune hepatitis, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution, with variable onset times that may occur months after initiating treatment. Pregnant individuals exposed to doravirine are encouraged to register with the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) to monitor pregnancy outcomes. Data on drug-associated risks to pregnancy outcomes are currently unavailable. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises against breastfeeding for HIV-infected women due to the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, potential viral resistance, and adverse reactions in breastfed infants. Women taking doravirine should not breastfeed. Doravirine should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted between 15–30°C (59–86°F). The medication should remain in its original bottle, tightly closed, and protected from moisture. Desiccants should not be removed. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as possible unless it is almost time for the next dose. In such cases, the next dose should be taken at the regularly scheduled time, and double dosing should be avoided.
